title: Gravitational Potential; Gravitational Potential Energy
notes: Gravitational Potential: Gravitational potential $V$ at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a test mass from infinity to that point: $V = W/m = -GM/r$. It is a scalar quantity with SI unit J/kg. Potential is zero at infinity (reference) and negative everywhere else.

Gravitational Potential Energy: Potential energy $U$ of mass $m$ at a point where potential is $V$: $U = mV = -GMm/r$. Near Earth's surface ($h \ll R$): $U = mgh$ (relative to surface). Change in PE: $\Delta U = mg\Delta h$.
Work Done by Gravitational Force: Work done in moving mass $m$ from $r_1$ to $r_2$: $W = -\Delta U = GMm(1/r_2 - 1/r_1)$. Work is path-independent (conservative force).
Gravitational Field and Potential Relation: $\vec{g} = -\nabla V$ or $g = -dV/dr$ for radial field. Field points in direction of decreasing potential.
Potential Due to Spherical Shell: Outside ($r > R$): $V = -GM/r$. Inside ($r < R$): $V = -GM/R$ (constant, equal to surface value). Field inside is zero but potential is not zero.
Potential Due to Solid Sphere: Outside ($r > R$): $V = -GM/r$. Inside ($r \le R$): $V = -\frac{GM}{2R^3}(3R^2 - r^2)$. At center: $V = -3GM/2R$.

Escape Velocity: Minimum speed to escape to infinity from surface: $v_\text{esc} = \sqrt{2GM/R} = \sqrt{2gR}$. For Earth: $\approx 11.2\text{ km/s}$. Derived from energy conservation: $\frac{1}{2}mv^2 - GMm/R = 0$.
Gravitational Potential is Scalar: Unlike field (vector), potential adds algebraically. Potential at a point due to multiple masses: $V = -\sum Gm_i/r_i$.
specificConditions: Reference at Infinity: Potential is defined with $V(\infty) = 0$. This makes all finite-distance potentials negative — work must be done to separate masses.
Near-Surface Approximation: $U = mgh$ is valid only for $h \ll R$ where $g$ is approximately constant. For large heights, use $U = -GMm/r$.
Potential is Not Field: Potential is scalar (can be negative), field is vector. $\vec{g} = -\nabla V$ — field points toward lower potential.
keyPoints: Gravitational potential $V = -GM/r$ (scalar, J/kg, zero at infinity).
Potential is scalar — add algebraically for multiple masses.
$\vec{g} = -\nabla V$ — field points toward decreasing potential.
Shell: potential constant inside, $-GM/R$; field zero inside.
importantStatements: Statement 1: Gravitational potential at a point is work done per unit mass bringing a test mass from infinity: $V = -GM/r$.
Statement 2: Gravitational potential energy is $U = -GMm/r$; near Earth's surface $U \approx mgh$.
Statement 3: Gravitational field is negative gradient of potential: $\vec{g} = -\nabla V$.
Statement 4: Potential is a scalar — potential due to multiple masses adds algebraically.
Statement 5: Escape velocity is $v_\text{esc} = \sqrt{2GM/R}$ — minimum speed to reach infinity with zero kinetic energy.
importantNotes: Potential is negative because gravity is attractive — work must be done against gravity to move mass to infinity.
Reference point for potential is arbitrary; only differences matter physically. Infinity = 0 is conventional.
Inside a spherical shell, field is zero but potential is constant ($-GM/R$) — not zero.
Escape velocity is independent of the escaping object's mass.
examShortTricks: Near surface: use $U = mgh$; far from Earth: use $U = -GMm/r$.
Escape velocity: $v_\text{esc} = \sqrt{2gR}$ — no need for G and M if g and R known.
Potential is scalar — just add values, no vector components.
Orbital velocity is $\sqrt{2}$ times smaller than escape velocity at same radius.
examNotes: NEB frequently asks for derivation of gravitational potential and potential energy.
Distinguish potential (scalar, J/kg) from potential energy (scalar, J) and field (vector, N/kg).
Escape velocity derivation using energy conservation is a standard question.
Shell theorem results: field = 0 inside, potential = constant inside shell.
examples: PE of 2 kg mass at Earth's surface: $U = mV = 2 \times (-6.25 \times 10^7) = -1.25 \times 10^8\text{ J}$.
Escape velocity from Earth: $v_\text{esc} = \sqrt{2 \times 9.8 \times 6.4\times 10^6} = 11{}200\text{ m/s} = 11.2\text{ km/s}$.
PE change lifting 5 kg by 10 m: $\Delta U = mgh = 5 \times 9.8 \times 10 = 490\text{ J}$.
practiceQuestions: Q1. Define gravitational potential and gravitational potential energy. State SI units.
Q2. Derive $V = -GM/r$ for gravitational potential due to a point mass.
Q3. Show that escape velocity is $v_\text{esc} = \sqrt{2GM/R}$ using energy conservation.
Q4. Calculate gravitational potential at Earth's surface given $M = 5.97\times 10^{24}\text{ kg}$, $R = 6.4\times 10^6\text{ m}$.
Q5. Distinguish between gravitational potential and gravitational potential energy.
Q6. Find potential inside and outside a thin spherical shell of mass M and radius R.
Q7. A 10 kg mass is moved from Earth's surface to height 2R. Find change in potential energy.
practice: Calculate gravitational potential due to point mass and spherical bodies.
Compute potential energy changes using $U = -GMm/r$ or $mgh$ as appropriate.
Derive and apply escape velocity formula.
Use relation $\vec{g} = -\nabla V$ to find field from potential.
Solve problems involving potential inside/outside spherical shells and solid spheres.
Calculate work done in moving masses in gravitational fields.
universalFacts: Gravitational potential energy is negative because gravity is attractive — bound systems have negative total energy.
Escape velocity from Earth (11.2 km/s) is much higher than orbital velocity (7.9 km/s) — escaping requires $\sqrt{2}$ times orbital speed.
Gravitational potential is a scalar — no direction, unlike gravitational field which is a vector.
The gravitational potential at the center of Earth is $-3GM/2R$ — about 1.5 times the surface value (more negative).
Black holes have escape velocity exceeding speed of light — nothing, not even light, can escape.
confusion: Confusing potential (V, J/kg) with potential energy (U, J): $U = mV$ — multiply by mass.
Thinking potential is always positive: Gravitational potential is negative (infinity = 0 reference).
Believing field inside shell is zero means potential is also zero: Field = 0 but potential = constant ($-GM/R$).
Using $mgh$ for large heights: Valid only for $h \ll R$; use $-GMm/r$ for space problems.
Confusing escape velocity with orbital velocity: $v_\text{esc} = \sqrt{2}\,v_\text{orb}$ at same radius.

summary: Gravitational potential $V = -GM/r$ is work per unit mass from infinity; potential energy $U = mV = -GMm/r$ (or $mgh$ near surface). Potential is scalar and negative; field $\vec{g} = -\nabla V$ points toward lower potential. Escape velocity $v_\text{esc} = \sqrt{2GM/R}$ is the minimum speed to escape to infinity.
